quartiers:Place de la Liberté and the ar.name: Place de la Liberté and the arcades
quartiers:Place de la Liberté and the ar.teaser: A long street of 146 stone arcades, rebuilt after the fire of 1637, ending at a clock tower
quartiers:Place de la Liberté and the ar.story: Rue du Commerce is Lons under cover: a run of 146 arcades in pale Jura stone, put back up through the 17th century after the fire of 1637, so you can walk its length dry in November rain. Shopfronts sit deep in the shade of the vaults; at the south end the Tour de l'Horloge, built from the stones of an older watchtower. At no. 24 is the house where Rouget de Lisle was born, and Bartholdi's bronze of him, dated 1882, stands at the Place de la Chevalerie crossroads a few minutes away, right arm raised. It was taken for metal by the occupiers in January 1942.
quartiers:Place de la Liberté and the ar.why: Walk the arcades early, before the shops open, when the vaults are empty and the first light comes in low.
facts: The covered walk under the arcades, the clock tower and the town's shops under one roof

quartiers:Place de la Comédie and the ma.name: Place de la Comédie and the market squares
quartiers:Place de la Comédie and the ma.teaser: Thursday is the day: clothes and tools on one square, cheese and Morteau on the next
quartiers:Place de la Comédie and the ma.story: On a Thursday the centre of Lons turns into the largest market in the department. The food goes up in the morning on the Place de Verdun, the hardware, clothes and household stalls fill the Place du 11 Novembre all day, and the theatre looks down on both: a rococo house rebuilt in 1901 after a fire and restored in 1997. Come with a cool bag and you will hear the plateau and the Bresse in the accents behind the trestles. The layout may change: in June 2026 the new mayor, Cyrille Brero, tested moving the non-food stalls onto Place de la Liberté and rue du Commerce.
quartiers:Place de la Comédie and the ma.why: Thursday morning is the one to plan the shore day around; the other markets are smaller.
facts: The Thursday market and the squares around the theatre

quartiers:The Parc des Bains and the Sou.name: The Parc des Bains and the Source Salée
quartiers:The Parc des Bains and the Sou.teaser: Seven hectares of old trees around a spa that still pipes in the town's salt water
quartiers:The Parc des Bains and the Sou.story: The Parc des Bains is where Lons tried to become a spa town. Seven hectares of trees gathered from five continents, a bandstand from about 1900, and a modern Korean garden on the extension. At its heart are the Thermes Lédonia, still using the salt water: a panoramic pool kept at 32°C, a hammam and a sauna, with cures for joints and skin. The name goes back to Ledonia, the spring the Romans worked, later called the Puits-Salé. Lons never got official spa-resort status after the First World War, for reasons of hygiene, which explains the modest scale. On an autumn morning mist lifts off the brine basin.
quartiers:The Parc des Bains and the Sou.why: Book a session in the warm salt pool at the Thermes after a cold morning on the slope.
facts: The tree park, the Source Salée basin and a swim in the Thermes Lédonia salt pool
Early on an autumn morning, when mist rises off the basin

quartiers:Arbois.name: Arbois
quartiers:Arbois.teaser: The Jura's wine town, cut in two by the Cuisance under a 60 m bell tower
quartiers:Arbois.story: Arbois calls itself the capital of Jura wine and the shop windows agree: tasting rooms and cellar doors around the arcaded Place de la Liberté. Walk down to the Cuisance, which cuts the town almost in two, and take the chemin de la Platière on the left bank for the view back to Saint-Just. The church goes back to the early 12th century, its vaults and choir to the 13th, and its bell tower, about 60 m high, carries eleven bells cast in 1738, the largest of them over four tonnes. At the start of September the town hangs a giant bunch of grapes in the nave for the Biou.
quartiers:Arbois.why: Lunch by the river, then walk the Platière path for the town's best view of Saint-Just.
facts: Cellar doors on the square, the Cuisance banks and the church of Saint-Just
Late morning for the tasting rooms; late afternoon on the river path

quartiers:Pupillin.name: Pupillin
quartiers:Pupillin.teaser: A hill village above Arbois that signs itself the world capital of Ploussard
quartiers:Pupillin.story: Pupillin sits a short climb above Arbois, a small village of cellar doors ringed by vines. The welcome signs call it the world capital of Ploussard, the pale local red; the AOC decrees spell it Poulsard, and here you will see both. The growers' cooperative, the Fruitière Vinicole de Pupillin, brings together about 35 families and keeps its tasting room open all year on rue du Ploussard. Pierre Overnoy and Emmanuel Houillon farm here, and La Table du Grapiot, opposite the mairie, took its first Michelin star in March 2026. A marked village trail loops through the vines.
quartiers:Pupillin.why: Taste a line of Ploussards at the Fruitière, then walk the village trail through the vines.
facts: Ploussard at its source, the cooperative cellar and the vineyard trail

quartiers:Château-Chalon.name: Château-Chalon
quartiers:Château-Chalon.teaser: A rock-top village of noblewomen's abbey stones above a slope that makes only Vin Jaune
quartiers:Château-Chalon.story: Château-Chalon grew around an abbey of Benedictine noblewomen and still has the feel of a fortified rock: tight lanes and the church of Saint-Pierre, Romanesque in origin. It is one of the Plus Beaux Villages de France. The village story credits the nuns with planting Savagnin and picking it late, which is tradition, not record. Below, the AOC Château-Chalon, about 50 ha across four communes, allows one wine only, Vin Jaune. Four signed viewpoints, Ménétru, la Roche, la Rochette and Saint-Jean, look over the terraces. The Maison de la Haute Seille, in the abbey's old guesthouse, holds exhibitions and pours the local wines.
quartiers:Château-Chalon.why: Walk out to the Roche viewpoint and see the whole Vin Jaune slope at your feet.
facts: The village lanes, the viewpoints over the vines and a Vin Jaune at the source

curiosities:The salt under the town.name: The salt under the town
curiosities:The salt under the town.teaser: Lons is named for its salt: the Romans worked the spring, and saltworks ran into the 1890s
curiosities:The salt under the town.story: The town is built over Triassic rock salt, and brine still finds its way up through the faults. People lived by the salt spring from the Neolithic; at the Étang du Saloir, on the Montmorot side, salt-making is attested from the Bronze Age. The Gaulish Sequani settled by the spring, the Romans worked the main source, Ledonia, later the Puits-Salé, and the town became Lons-le-Saunier, saunier being the salt-maker. In 1743 a royal decree founded the Montmorot saltworks, built 1744 to 1752; another plant at Montaigu started in 1893 and was making 2,500 tonnes a year by 1895.
curiosities:The salt under the town.why: Every street name with 'salé' or 'saline' in it is a trace of what paid for this town.
facts: The 18th-century saltworks buildings at Montmorot on the western edge of town (restored), and the brine itself in the Parc des Bains basin and the Thermes Lédonia pool

curiosities:Savagnin's family tree.name: Savagnin's family tree
curiosities:Savagnin's family tree.teaser: The Jura's white grape, Traminer by another name, sits behind Sauvignon Blanc and Grüner Veltliner
curiosities:Savagnin's family tree.story: Savagnin is the Jura's name for Traminer, and DNA has put it near the root of half the white-wine list. Austrian work in the late 1990s found Traminer as one parent of Grüner Veltliner; the other turned out to be a single neglected vine at St. Georgen am Leithagebirge, near Eisenstadt, found in 2000 and confirmed in 2007, officially named Mater Veltlinis in 2023. Sauvignon Blanc and Chenin Blanc each show a parent-offspring link with Savagnin, which makes Savagnin a grandparent of Cabernet Sauvignon, a Sauvignon Blanc and Cabernet Franc cross. Gewürztraminer is its aromatic, pink-skinned form.
curiosities:Savagnin's family tree.why: Pour an ouillé Savagnin next to a Sauvignon Blanc and look for the family resemblance.
facts: Order a Savagnin ouillé (topped-up, fresh) beside one aged sous voile (walnut and curry): the same grape, two styles; about EUR 18-45 a bottle (seen May 2026)

DNA shows a parent-offspring link but not its direction: Savagnin is taken as the parent of Sauvignon and Chenin from history, not genetics, and one glossary says an earlier suspected Savagnin x Chenin pedigree was disproved. The old guide's 'UC Davis/INRA 1999' credit could not be confirmed

curiosities:Arbois in the first gazette.name: Arbois in the first gazette
curiosities:Arbois in the first gazette.teaser: On 15 May 1936 France named its first six AOCs, and Arbois heads the list
curiosities:Arbois in the first gazette.story: The 1935 law created the appellation d'origine contrôlée; the first decrees came on 15 May 1936, a day after the agriculture minister's report on Châteauneuf-du-Pape cleared the way. Six names went through: Arbois, Cassis, Châteauneuf-du-Pape, Cognac, Monbazillac and Tavel. Arbois sits first on the alphabetical list, and from there grew the local line that the Jura holds France's oldest appellation. The campaign behind the law was led by the Rhône grower Baron Pierre Le Roy de Boiseaumarié and the Bordeaux senator Joseph Capus. All six turned 90 in 2026, and INAO marked the anniversary in February.
curiosities:Arbois in the first gazette.why: Read 'Appellation Arbois Contrôlée' on a label as a date: May 1936, among the first six in France.
facts: Any bottle labelled Arbois or Arbois-Pupillin: taste one at the Caveau des Jacobins in Lons or at a cellar door in Arbois

Arbois's 'first AOC in France' is a local and guidebook claim; INAO dates all six to the same day, and Châteauneuf-du-Pape points to the minister's report on its case, dated 14 May 1936. The old guide's inclusion of Vosne-Romanée was wrong: the sixth was Cognac

curiosities:Rouget de Lisle.name: Rouget de Lisle
curiosities:Rouget de Lisle.teaser: The man who wrote the Marseillaise was born above a shop under the Lons arcades
curiosities:Rouget de Lisle.story: Claude-Joseph Rouget de Lisle was born at 24 rue du Commerce on 10 May 1760. A young engineering officer, he wrote the Chant de guerre pour l'armée du Rhin in Strasbourg in April 1792; troops from Marseille carried it north and it took their city's name. The family apartment is now a small museum, the Maison Rouget de Lisle, built on the donation of André Lançon and a Maison des Illustres since 2011, with an old lime tree in the courtyard. In 2026 the town marked 190 years since his death in 1836 with free summer visits.
curiosities:Rouget de Lisle.why: Stand in the narrow rooms where he was born, then walk to his statue: the anthem feels smaller and closer.
facts: 10 May 1760, 24 rue du Commerce, Lons-le-Saunier; died 1836

culture:Saint-Désiré and its crypt.name: Saint-Désiré and its crypt
culture:Saint-Désiré and its crypt.teaser: Below the choir, an 11th-century crypt holds the empty stone coffin of the town's patron saint
culture:Saint-Désiré and its crypt.story: Saint-Désiré is the oldest standing layer of Lons. The church is Romanesque, and the crypt under the choir survives from the first half of the 11th century: low vaults, cold air, a smell of damp stone. In its apse lies the sarcophagus of Saint Désiré, patron of the town. It is empty: his relics were moved and are now kept across the centre in the church of the Cordeliers. A 16th-century statue of a bishop, taken to be the saint, was restored and set down here beside it. The crypt was restored in 1992; the church has been a listed monument since 1908.
culture:Saint-Désiré and its crypt.why: Go down into the crypt: ten minutes underground and you are a thousand years back.
facts: Church open for free visits; crypt hours not published: check with the tourist office (group guided visits on request, tel. 03 84 24 65 01)

culture:Église des Cordeliers.name: Église des Cordeliers
culture:Église des Cordeliers.teaser: A burned and rebuilt Franciscan church that keeps the relics of Lons's patron saint
culture:Église des Cordeliers.story: The Franciscans arrived in the 13th century, but fire after fire means what you see is mostly 18th-century: a Jesuit-style front finished in 1731, still carrying its revolutionary inscription, a carved pulpit of 1728, choir stalls from about 1828 and a large Callinet organ of around 1845. Under the floor, in a crypt now closed, lie the Chalon family, the lords of the town. In 1531 Philiberte de Luxembourg ordered an alabaster tomb for Jean IV de Chalon-Arlay and his kin from the sculptors Conrad Meyt and Giovanni-Battista Mariotto. The relics of Saint Désiré, whose empty coffin is at his own church, are kept here.
culture:Église des Cordeliers.why: Read the revolutionary words on the facade, then sit under the Callinet organ in the quiet.
facts: Free visits during opening hours (times not published); paid guided visits for groups of five or more via the tourist office, tel. 03 84 24 65 01

culture:La Maison de la Vache qui rit.name: La Maison de la Vache qui rit
culture:La Maison de la Vache qui rit.teaser: A laughing cow first painted on army supply trucks became a cheese brand born in Lons
culture:La Maison de la Vache qui rit.story: The cow began in the trenches. In the First World War Benjamin Rabier drew a grinning cow for the meat-supply trucks of the unit nicknamed the Wachkyrie, a joke on Wagner's Valkyries. Léon Bel had served with it, and in 1921 in Lons he registered La Vache qui rit for his processed cheese, a fromage fondu. The red cow with the cheese-box earrings followed in 1923 or 1924. The museum on rue Richebourg tells a century of the brand through its design and advertising, and was refreshed for the 2021 centenary. The Caveau des Jacobins is on the same street.
culture:La Maison de la Vache qui rit.why: Look for the earrings on the old boxes: each one shows the cow wearing her own box.
facts: 2023 timetable, not yet confirmed for 2026: November-December weekends only 14:00-18:00, daily 10:00-18:00 in school holidays, closed in January; outside holidays Tue-Sun 14:00-18:00 from February to October

culture:The Saline Royale.name: The Saline Royale
culture:The Saline Royale.teaser: Ledoux's half-moon royal saltworks, fed by brine piped in from Salins through the forest
culture:The Saline Royale.story: Claude-Nicolas Ledoux designed Arc-et-Senans as a factory that looks like a city: workshops and workers' houses set in a semicircle, the Director's House at the centre, where every line of the plan meets. It was built from 1775, worked from 1779 and closed in 1895. The site was chosen for the Chaux forest, which fed the boilers, while the brine came from Salins-les-Bains through a wooden pipe of about 21 km, replaced with cast iron from 1782. UNESCO listed it in 1982 and added Salins in 2009. From 1 November the gardens are bare and the visit is indoors and out, 10:00 to 17:00.
culture:The Saline Royale.why: Stand in the Director's House doorway and see the whole semicircle wheel around you.

culture:Maison de Louis Pasteur.name: Maison de Louis Pasteur
culture:Maison de Louis Pasteur.teaser: The Arbois family house on the Cuisance where Pasteur kept a working laboratory
culture:Maison de Louis Pasteur.story: The Pasteur family moved to this house in Arbois in 1827, when Louis was four, and he kept coming back to it. The house is kept as the family knew it, with his laboratory preserved inside, one of the Maisons des Illustres. A myth here says he took his doctorate on Vin Jaune. In fact the 1847 thesis was on crystallography; the 1857 paper on lactic fermentation showed living organisms at work, and the gentle heating of wine came from his Études sur le vin of 1866. His vineyard, the 44-are Clos de Rosières at Montigny-lès-Arsures, belongs to the Académie des sciences.
culture:Maison de Louis Pasteur.why: See the laboratory: the room where wine spoilage was treated as a science.

culture:Musée d'Archéologie du Jura.name: Musée d'Archéologie du Jura
culture:Musée d'Archéologie du Jura.teaser: The Jura's lake-village finds are in storage while Lons rebuilds its museums
culture:Musée d'Archéologie du Jura.story: Do not plan on this one. The archaeology museum of Lons has no galleries open: since 2010 its collections have been kept in the external stores of the Centre de conservation et d'étude René-Rémond, and the team is working on a reopening as part of a joint refoundation of the archaeology and fine-arts museums. No date has been announced. That is a loss, because the collection holds the Neolithic finds from the lakes of Chalain and the plateau, wooden tools and organic remains kept for thousands of years in lake mud. For now the museum shows itself through school workshops and short exhibitions.
culture:Musée d'Archéologie du Jura.why: Skip it for now; see the lake country itself on a plateau day instead.
facts: Closed: collections in storage since 2010, reopening project with no date (Oct 2026)
